name: Tekton
summary: Building blocks for CI/CD systems as Kubernetes resources: each Task runs as a pod, each step in it as a container, and Pipelines chain Tasks together.
intro: Tekton Pipelines installs into a Kubernetes cluster and adds custom resources. A `Task` is an ordered list of steps, and each step names a container image and a command or script. When a `TaskRun` starts the Task, Tekton creates one pod for it with one container per step, run in order until the first failure. A `Pipeline` arranges Tasks into a graph, and a `PipelineRun` runs it. Because every Task gets its own pod, Tasks share nothing by default: files travel between them through workspaces, which are volumes, and small values through results, whose size is capped by Kubernetes’ container termination message.

Pipelines is the core of a set of components, aimed at platform teams building CI/CD for their developers rather than at developers directly. Triggers starts runs from events such as a merged pull request, Pipelines-as-Code reads definitions from a `.tekton/` directory in the repository, `tkn` is the command line, the Dashboard a web UI, and Chains records provenance for what a run built and signs it with keys from cosign or a KMS, or keylessly through Sigstore. Red Hat OpenShift Pipelines and IBM Cloud Continuous Delivery are built on it. Pipelines reached 1.0 in May 2025 and ships monthly, with four releases a year supported long term; the latest is 1.17.1, from October 2026. Tekton was a graduated project of the Continuous Delivery Foundation and moved to the CNCF as an incubating project in March 2026.
strengths: Everything is a Kubernetes resource, so pipelines are applied, versioned and secured like any other workload, with no separate CI server
Any container image can be a step, and each Task runs in its own pod, isolated from other runs
Reusable Tasks and Pipelines can be shared across teams and pulled from the community Catalog
Supply-chain features built in: Chains signs build results and records SLSA provenance
limits: Needs a Kubernetes cluster, and every Task pays for starting a pod
Tasks share no files by default: data must go through workspaces or results, and results are limited in size
A toolkit rather than a finished product: triggers, UI and repository integration are separate components, and the project calls its Dashboard a work in progress
Releases other than the four LTS lines a year are supported for about a month, so clusters need regular upgrades

story: By 2018 many CI/CD systems ran on Kubernetes, and each rebuilt the same basic machinery for running build steps in containers. Engineers at Google, among them Dan Lorenc, sketched a set of shared resources inside the Knative project in August 2018; the code lived in `knative/build-pipeline`, and the aim, in Lorenc’s words, was to “make the hard parts of building CI/CD systems easy”.

In February 2019, just before its 0.1 release, the team split the project out of Knative, named it Tekton and gave it to the new Continuous Delivery Foundation, where it was a founding project in March. Knative Build was deprecated in favour of Tekton Pipelines that June. Tekton graduated at the CDF in October 2022 after an independent security audit, and Pipelines reached 1.0 in May 2025, after its v1 API had been stable for more than two years.

In March 2026 the CNCF accepted Tekton as an incubating project, putting it alongside Kubernetes, Knative and Argo, which it already worked with. The project said nothing changed for users and that its governance and infrastructure would move to CNCF processes over time.

choices.choice: Building blocks, not a CI product
choices.why: Many Kubernetes CI/CD systems were rebuilding the same infrastructure. Tekton aimed to be the common layer underneath, so it defines resources and controllers and leaves user interfaces and opinions to the products built on top, such as OpenShift Pipelines.

choices.choice: A Task is a pod and a step is a container
choices.why: Reusing Kubernetes’ own scheduling and isolation meant any container image could be a build step, and each run is kept apart from others in its own pod.

choices.choice: Kubernetes custom resources as the API
choices.why: Defining Tasks and Pipelines as resources lets teams apply, secure and audit them with the same tools and RBAC they already use for everything else in the cluster.
